11 — Clean outer-fold Does image uncertainty help prioritise review?

Version 2 reporting boundary. Primary ranking is unweighted mean outer-fold ROC-AUC; AP is secondary. An inner-validation pilot or uncertainty experiment has no five-fold estimate, so its ROC-AUC is explicitly exploratory. The saved image recipes, AP-selected checkpoints/epochs and AP-based admission gates remain unchanged and are labelled historical selection rules. This is a presentation migration, not a ROC-selected image refit. Executing every cell reads saved artifacts and writes only new v2 reports: no image smoke, checkpoint inference, training, calibration fitting, cutoff selection, final all-development fit or reserved-test access occurs. The added metadata experiment uses its own explicit v2 ROC selection identity.

An image model produces a score between 0 and 1: higher means more strongly ranked toward melanoma. Uncertainty here means how much that score varies when we repeat prediction under specified changes. A high score and a high uncertainty estimate answer different questions.

We test whether variation improves the order in which images are sent for review, beyond simply sending the highest ordinary scores. The saved clean inference used each image's own outer-held-out B0 checkpoint (saved model weights), from a fresh fixed-duration refit. The report loads exported predictions and receipts only: it does not rebuild a network, choose an old best checkpoint or perform inference. An epoch is one pass through the fitting data.

These are five-fold outer-held-out diagnostics: each scored patient's images were excluded from that checkpoint's fitting, recipe and duration selection. This strengthens the original one-inner-split scope. Earlier development exploration remains a limitation; uncertainty rankings still do not select a clinical referral policy or final architecture. The reserved test comes last and is never opened by this report.

The historical three-epoch experiment and its result files are preserved. Clean pass exports belong to results/dedup_v1/uncertainty/b0_uncertainty_dedup_v1; executing this notebook regenerates only its separate clean presentation figures. See the concept guide when a term is unfamiliar.

Deduplicated workflow adaptation. This notebook uses the frozen dedup_v1 development manifest and original patient assignments. It reads saved clean artifacts; executing it starts no training and does not load the reserved test. The original notebook is preserved as the presentation template: 13_image_uncertainty.ipynb.

Genuine experiment-scope change: clean matching outer-refit predictions replace the historical one-inner-split selected checkpoint. Colours, referral linestyles, two-panel convergence, five-bin reliability, histogram composition and MC-circle/TTA-square intervals retain the original visual language.

1. Choose saved clean checkpoints explicitly

The clean inference receipts identify one fresh outer refit per preserved fold. They record the exact run, recipe (training settings), selected fixed duration, checkpoint hash (file fingerprint), source-image identities, deterministic preparation and saved ordinary predictions. All five raw refits must complete before full clean uncertainty is accepted. Missing or incompatible artifacts stop verification rather than silently falling back to a historical model.

Scope change: the original selectable one-pilot checkpoint adapter is replaced by recorded b0_nested_dedup_v1 outer checkpoints. This is an explicit matching clean inference scope, not automatic architecture selection. SOURCE_RUN, architecture and recipe are provenance for every fold, not notebook settings that trigger another inference run. The table below reads actual completion; no checkpoint is loaded into a neural network by this notebook.

def show_saved_table(relative, limit=30):
    path = project_path(ROOT, relative)
    if not path.exists():
        display(Markdown("**Pending:** " + relative + ". No results are inferred from unfinished runs."))
        return pd.DataFrame()
    table = pd.read_csv(path)
    display(table.head(limit))
    if len(table) > limit:
        display(Markdown(f"Showing {limit} of {len(table)} rows; the complete CSV is saved."))
    return table

def comparison_table():
    evaluation = latest_evaluation(ROOT)
    if "output_directory" not in evaluation:
        display(Markdown("**Pending:** clean evaluation has not been generated."))
        return pd.DataFrame()
    path = project_path(ROOT, evaluation["output_directory"] + "/model_comparison.csv")

def model_chart(table, title):
    if table.empty:
        display(Markdown("**Pending:** no verified scores are available for this stage."))
        return
    table = table.sort_values("roc_auc")
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, max(3.2, .38 * len(table) + 1.5)), layout="constrained")
    ax.barh(table.model, table.roc_auc, color="#276b91")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Unweighted mean outer-fold ROC-AUC", xlim=(0, max(.1, float(table.roc_auc.max()) * 1.25)))
    finish_figure(fig, "model_comparison_roc_auc")

def pilot_report(run_id):
    directory = ROOT / "results/image_d1_runs" / run_id
    path = directory / "summary.json"
    summary = read_json(path) if path.exists() else {"status": "pending"}
    if summary.get("status") == "complete":
        manifest = read_json(directory / "run_manifest.json")
        if manifest["dataset_identity"] != dataset_identity:
            raise ValueError("Pilot belongs to another dataset.")
        from melanoma_detection.development_dataset import sha256_file
        for relative, digest in summary["artifact_sha256"].items():
            artifact = (directory / relative).resolve()
            if not artifact.is_relative_to(directory.resolve()) or sha256_file(artifact) != digest:
                raise ValueError("Completed pilot artifact changed.")
    return directory, summary

3. Check a small sample before full inference

The smoke check uses 16 images to catch a mismatch before a costly full run. Deterministic predictions must repeat and agree with the saved export. Two seeded dropout passes must vary under different seeds and repeat under the same seed. Only explicit dropout may activate; BatchNorm buffers and all model state must stay unchanged. Identity TTA (no image change) must reproduce the ordinary score. Any failure stopped the separate clean inference runner before its 30-pass run. This notebook reads its recorded smoke checks; it does not rerun inference or mutate model state. The completed receipts are shown below when available.

4. Keep dropout variation and image-view variation separate

MC dropout (Monte Carlo dropout) predicts the same prepared image 30 times. Dropout randomly disables some activations, creating a different mask each pass. Only explicit dropout layers activate at their trained rate (0.2 here). BatchNorm, which keeps learned normalisation statistics, and stochastic depth, which can randomly bypass network blocks, stay in evaluation mode. Every pass has a recorded seed. The mean is an ensemble prediction score; sample standard deviation (SD, denominator 29) measures spread under those masks. It does not capture all sources of uncertainty.

TTA (test-time augmentation) instead keeps the whole model in evaluation mode and averages four views: identity, horizontal, vertical and both flips. They act on the exact prepared tensor after whole-image resize and any recorded preprocessing. No crop, padding, arbitrary rotation or colour change is added. Flips preserve pixels and can be applied after normalisation without changing their values. Sample SD (denominator 3) measures orientation sensitivity for these four views, not uncertainty across every plausible image change. Its numerical size cannot be compared with dropout SD as total uncertainty.

Sigmoid converts the network output to a score in [0,1]. These scores and their means are not calibrated probabilities: class weighting can change their scale. No score-to-probability mapping or decision threshold is fitted here.

Only complete, validated raw predictions enter a summary. The saved raw tables allow every mean and SD to be independently recomputed.

6. Check stability as the number of passes increases

Compare the first 5, 10 and 20 seeded passes with the same 30-pass reference; labels do not select the pass count. Read the two panels: pass count is horizontal. Left, mean absolute difference from the reference is vertical, with separate solid/ dashed lines for mean score and SD for each preserved fold; closer to zero means more stable values. Right, SD rank correlation is vertical; closer to 1 means a more similar ordering of images. The table also gives overlap among the highest-SD 20%. Fold colours identify the five different held-out checkpoints; the original two-panel composition and numerical-versus-ranking distinction are retained.

Stable scores need not imply stable rankings. The finite 30-pass reference is not an exact expectation, so agreement is evidence of stability rather than proof that all uncertainty has been captured.

7. Compare ranking and descriptive reliability

AP (average precision) summarises precision (malignancy among flags) as recall (malignant images found) changes with the cutoff; higher is better. It is useful for rare malignancies. ROC-AUC summarises overall ranking; higher is better and 0.5 is chance. Log loss penalises confident wrong scores and Brier averages squared score errors; lower is better, but both can hide poor recall when benign images dominate. The fitting-prevalence constant is a simple baseline computed without validation labels, not a fitted calibrator.

Read the reliability diagram: each line is deterministic, MC mean or TTA mean. Up to five equal-count bins group similar scores. Horizontal position is the bin's mean score, vertical position its observed malignant-image fraction. The diagonal means agreement; below it scores exceed the observed frequency, above it scores fall below it. Left shows [0,1]; right enlarges the same observed range and bins. A point near the diagonal is descriptive agreement, not proof of calibrated clinical risk. Bin support is saved; sparse malignancies and patients contributing to several bins make the estimates noisy. Each checkpoint's duration was chosen within its own training patients. Scope change: these pooled diagrams use matching clean outer-held-out predictions, while unweighted mean-fold ROC-AUC is primary and AP is secondary. The earlier pilot/development adaptations still limit the independence of final claims.

8. Examine what the two SD measures capture

Read the histograms: the left panel bins MC score SD and the middle bins TTA score SD horizontally; vertical height counts images. Mass near zero means little change under that procedure. Each panel has its own SD scale because dropout masks and image orientations perturb different things.

Read the scatterplot: each dot is an image, with MC SD horizontally and TTA SD vertically. A rising pattern suggests the methods prioritise similar images; scatter suggests different sensitivities. There is no equal-SD target because the measures have different meanings. Variation does not prove malignancy or error, and a model can be consistently, confidently wrong.

9. Does SD improve the referral order?

Referral means setting some images aside for review. The retained set contains those still evaluated automatically. All rankings use the same deterministic predictions, labels and predeclared referral fractions, so the comparison isolates ranking rather than MC/TTA score averaging.

Rank from highest to lowest by SD, ordinary score, or predictive entropy −s log(s) − (1−s) log(1−s). Score ranking prioritises stronger melanoma scores; entropy prioritises scores near 0.5, where the binary score is least decisive. Entropy inherits the uncalibrated score scale. Random referral is repeated with 100 recorded seeds to give a simple baseline. Ties use image ID; no operational fraction is selected from these labels.

Retained classification error uses the fixed descriptive cutoff 0.5; MAE (mean absolute score error) and Brier also expose score errors. Malignant images referred and distinct patients with a malignant image referred have different denominators. Referral acts on images, not every image from a patient, and it does not simulate whether a reviewer diagnoses correctly.

Read the four panels: the top row uses MC SD, the bottom TTA SD. Horizontal position is percentage of all images referred. Left is retained classification error (lower is better); right is percentage of malignant images referred (higher is better). Lines compare SD, ordinary score, entropy and mean random referral at the same budget. Compare at the same horizontal position; a lower left curve alone may hide which malignant cases remain. These curves describe trade-offs, not a selected clinical policy.

10. Estimate paired differences with patient bootstrap intervals

The patient bootstrap repeatedly samples whole patient groups with replacement, keeping each patient's images together. We use 2,000 resamples of the original number of retained patients independently within each of the five outer folds and recompute referral rankings and budgets each time. This respects dependence between images of the same patient. Differences are SD ranking minus score, entropy or mean random ranking on the same resample. Undefined malignant fractions in resamples without malignancy remain missing; valid replicate counts are reported.

Read the interval plot at the predeclared 20% referral: each row names the method and comparator. Dots/squares are paired estimates, horizontal bars are 95% percentile intervals; blue circles are MC and orange squares TTA. Horizontal units are percentage-point differences. The dotted zero line means no difference. On the left, negative retained-error differences favour SD; on the right, positive malignant-referral differences favour SD. An interval crossing zero includes no difference and should not be read as clear evidence of benefit.

Intervals describe uncertainty conditional on these fitted predictions and finite masks/views. They omit training-seed variation and do not include retraining or repeat the recipe/duration selection process, and do not undo earlier development adaptation. Testing several fractions also creates multiple comparisons; a favourable point does not establish a referral policy.

11. Preserve the training artifacts and record provenance

File hashes compare checkpoints, histories, old prototype outputs and the historical notebook in the saved before/after inference receipts. We also retain the checkpoint and split identities, deterministic preprocessing profile, all pass seeds, batch size, device and package versions, referral seeds/fractions, bootstrap settings and the current inference source hashes. Raw and summary outputs belong only to the clean inference directory. Figure outputs belong to this notebook's separate clean report directory; no source checkpoint, saved raw pass or historical result is overwritten.

Limitations

This is a complete but imbalanced retained five-fold development cohort. Each scored patient is excluded from its own checkpoint's recipe/duration selection, and direct training leakage is checked. Earlier development pilots and model exploration mean this still cannot replace an independent final test. Neither a favourable architecture AP nor a favourable referral fraction selects the final model.

Dropout SD covers explicit dropout-mask variation only. It excludes backbone stochastic depth, training-seed variation and distribution shift. TTA covers four conservative orientations only; it does not estimate total uncertainty. Thirty passes are a finite reference, and rank convergence can be slower than score convergence. Low uncertainty can accompany consistent errors.

The class-weighted scores are uncalibrated. Reliability bins have sparse malignant support, and image-level referral does not establish patient-level clinical benefit. The fixed cutoff 0.5 is descriptive. Bootstrap intervals are conditional and do not correct selection optimism or multiple comparisons. No calibrator, selected clinical referral threshold, fusion model or reserved test evaluation is implemented by this report. The separate clean calibration stage remains distinct from these raw-score uncertainty diagnostics.

Summary

The current workflow attaches uncertainty to the explicitly recorded matching outer-refit checkpoints, reproduces its exact preparation and patient membership, and checks inference without changing training artifacts. Raw scores, MC means/SDs and TTA means/SDs are kept separate and saved with provenance. The executed summary below reports the observed prediction metrics; the referral tables and paired intervals determine whether SD adds useful information on the retained outer-held-out records. All findings remain conditional development diagnostics. The numerical recap uses saved clean results; an unchanged frozen procedure and the independently reserved test remain necessary before claiming final generalisation.
